1:
The occasion is set before the letter is read. Clarke summarises the chapter as two letters, the first recommending patience under a captivity to last seventy years, the second denouncing the men who promised a speedy end to it, and dates the whole to the first or second year of Zedekiah; the prophet, hearing that those deported had been persuaded they would soon come home, feared they would take some hasty step. Ellicott names the same danger, a restless disquietude fostered by prophets urging revolt, and treats the letter as an earnest protest in line with all he had said before. Calvin gives the design a double object: to lighten the grief of the exiles and to break the obstinacy of those still at home, who thought themselves fortunate to have escaped and needed to learn that nothing would suit them better than joining their brethren.

Gill and Henry draw a lesson from the writing of a letter. Gill observes that prophets taught sometimes by sermons and sometimes by epistles, as the apostles afterwards did. Henry makes it a rule: what is written is as truly given by inspiration as what is spoken, and was the proper way of spreading the knowledge of God's will among children scattered abroad. He turns it into advice, that we may serve God by writing to distant friends what we cannot say, since what is written remains. On the deportation he notes that the surrender meant to pacify the conqueror did the opposite, the victor growing on their concessions as a king in an older story grew on another's.

The people carried away are identified with care. Henry lists the king, the queen his mother, the chamberlains called eunuchs here, the princes, and the carpenters and smiths, whose removal left those remaining without hands to fortify the city or make weapons; and their case looked the more melancholy because being singled out made them appear the greater sinners. Wesley distinguishes two deportations eleven or twelve years apart and assigns this to the earlier, when ten thousand went with the craftsmen and smiths. Ellicott identifies the queen as the queen-mother, allowing a possible family connection with another man in the book but refusing to assert it, and takes the phrase residue of the elders to show that the whole body of counsellors had not gone into exile, only the more prominent. Among the princes, he suggests, we are to think of Daniel and his companions.

The messengers interest Ellicott most. One was brother to the man who had once protected the prophet from being killed; the other was probably son to the high priest who found the lost book of the law and led the reformation under Josiah. Both would naturally stand among the prophet's friends, and carried his letter with the king's dispatch. From that he infers something about the king: sending envoys at all shows that the weak and vacillating ruler had been influenced by the prophet's counsel, had half abandoned revolt, and was acknowledging the overlordship of Babylon; a letter carried by royal envoys, he adds, is unlikely to have stood in flagrant antagonism to their mission.

Two smaller points stand against the text. Ellicott observes that the prophet's name is spelt in the opening verse in a shorter form than the book usually employs, and takes this as probably indicating that the sentence introducing the letter was a later hand's. Wesley explains the route more simply: the king had occasion to send two messengers, and the prophet, knowing there were men in Babylon feeding the people with hopes of a speedy return as there were at home, used the chance to quiet them. Calvin puts the aim in his own terms: they are to look to the end of the captivity, and meanwhile be patient and raise no tumults until God put forth his hand.
4:
Ellicott begins with the form. This is the nearest thing in the older scriptures to the letters that fill so much of the newer, the actual text of one sent to people the teacher could no longer speak to, and it plainly supplied the model for the apocryphal letter later fathered on him. Gill attends to the titles it opens with. The Lord of hosts commands the armies above and below, and can deliver by his own power, by armies raised on earth, or by legions of angels; the God of Israel is a covenant name still theirs in spite of their sins and their exile, serving to keep them from the idolatry of the country and to remind them who alone was to be worshipped. The prophet, he adds, was only the amanuensis.

The command to build houses is a date in disguise. Gill takes it to mean they must not look for a short stay but many years, and that they would be free to build and not be dispossessed. Clarke adds a purpose, that they provide the necessaries of life and multiply until they became a powerful people. Ellicott gives it a twofold bearing: it counsels patient acceptance and announces that the exile would run at least two generations; and men allowed to own land and houses were being handled with comparative leniency.

Calvin faces the objection that these look like contrary instructions. To live seventy years as though native to the place and yet always expect a return seems inconsistent, and his answer is that obedience and hope occupy different offices. Obedience meant owning the chastisement as God's and submitting for the whole term; hope was to hang in suspense, so they should neither fret nor be carried away by violent feeling. He guards it both ways. He is not encouraging them to settle in a fertile country and forget their own, since everything he says is confined to the term; but neither may they hurry it, because a man driven headlong by vehement desire in a manner repels God's favour, taking from him his rights and will, as though unwilling to receive the grace.

On marriage the comments are practical. Gill takes the command as addressed to those who had no wives, and specifies that they were not to take wives of the Chaldeans, intermarriage with the heathen being forbidden, but of their own nation, to keep up a succession. Calvin observes only that the prophet here speaks according to the usual order of nature.

Seeking the peace of the city is the difficult order. Ellicott calls it the hardest command in the letter: to give up all cursing, even the sort that came from the men who hung their harps on the willows, and to pray for the prosperity of the city where they ate the bread of captivity, needed a patience close to superhuman. He follows the thought where it leads: unless one distinguishes the times and puts that psalm at a different moment, its imprecations belong to a lower stage than the prophet's counsel. He sets the prophet beside the charge to pray for an emperor who was Nero. Clarke argues from plain interest: wherever a man lives and is fed is his country while he stays, and these exiles, not being in cruel servitude, were nearly as well placed as at home and better than the brethren they had left. Calvin presses further, holding that the words bind them to be faithful subjects and obey from the heart; and he settles the verb, since to seek can mean to pray but here means to care for and promote, as seeking a land means caring for it, so the clause requires active effort for the safety of the monarchy, the prayer following after. Gill keeps both halves, prayer and every other useful means.
8:
The warning against the prophets in Babylon shows the same trade plied in both places. Ellicott says as much: the agencies counteracting the prophet at home were at work among the exiles too, promising a speedy deliverance in a name that had not sent them. Gill notes that the pretence of divine authority was exactly what made the falsehood acceptable. Henry adds the reproach: so long as we have the word of truth to try the spirits by, being deceived is our own fault, since by it we may be undeceived.

The dreams are handled three ways. Clarke would not translate dreams but dreamers, since there was a class of men who had acquired a facility in the thing and undertook to interpret for others. Ellicott keeps the noun and fastens on the causative, calling the dreams which ye cause to be dreamed an exceptional phrase, and taking it to mean that the supply was created by the demand. Henry works the causative harder and both ways: they may be the people's own fancies, since men who think of nothing but a speedy release when awake will dream of it asleep and take the dream for an omen, or they may be the prophets' dreams, called the people's because the people wanted them and encouraged the flattery. False prophets, he concludes, would not flatter people in their sins if people did not love it.

Where the seventy years begin is settled by two of them the same way. Gill rules out the last captivity, the present moment and the first deportation, and dates them from the fourth year of Jehoiakim, when the conqueror first came against the city. Wesley reckons from the same point and draws the consequence, that eleven years had already run before the last king was carried off. Clarke stays with the words: the phrase is at the mouth of the accomplishment, or filled to the brim, so the whole seventy must be completed and no enlargement looked for.

Clarke also reports, without endorsing it, a proposal to rearrange the chapter: a very serious transposition of verses is supposed to have occurred, so that after the ninth verse one should read the sixteenth through the nineteenth, then the tenth through the fourteenth, then the twentieth, the fifteenth, the twenty-first, and on regularly. He leaves it standing beside the received order.

The thoughts of peace draw out each reader's temperament. Gill dwells on the security of a purpose held in the mind of God: men think and forget and their thoughts come to nothing, while his are remembered and cannot fail. Clarke sets the promise out as a numbered scheme: God's love was moved, he would perform his word, they must pray and seek and search, he would hearken and be found, and all of it turned on their seeking him with the whole heart. Ellicott corrects the translation instead. The familiar expected end is better rendered a future and a hope, which is what the words literally say and is far more expressive, since an expected end may be one a man shrinks from; the future tells them their history is not over, the hope that a better time is in store, and waiting for it rather than trusting delusive assurances was the exiles' true wisdom. Wesley builds on the older rendering rather than replacing it, taking the end promised as the very end they expect and desire, and grounding it on mercy to the seed of Abraham rather than merit. Calvin explains why so much is said at all: men fall into one of two extremes, rapt above the clouds by vain hopes or lying astonished in despair, and this people showed both, laughing at threatenings while at home and then, in exile, believing anyone who promised a quick return while rejecting with disdain the deliverance actually offered.
12:
The middle verb of the first clause divides Calvin from everyone he has read. Almost all take the word for going or walking as a moral term, so that the men who had wandered after their own lusts would now walk in the law; Calvin calls that too forced. He hears instead an indirect reproof of the people's slowness: to go, in this sentence, means little more than saying that after an exile not of one year but of seventy they will at last begin to be wise. What the verse records, on his reading, is that it took so long to subdue them, twenty or thirty years not being enough for a disposition so rude and refractory that failing to be brought to prayer by such scourges was not sloth merely but stupidity.

Gill takes the same clause as pure encouragement and reads the sequence the other way about. When God means to bestow a mercy he first gives his people a spirit of prayer to ask for it, so that the promise of the thing is itself a considerable argument for praying, and the praying is evidence that the time is near. He works the following verse out at length as a description of what seeking rightly involves: seeking in Christ, who is the only way to the Father, under the guidance of the Spirit, in the exercise of faith on him and on his promises, with fervency and ardour of mind, with diligence and importunity, with earnest desire and strong affection, and with all sincerity of soul. Where those conditions are met, he says flatly, men always find him.

Calvin arrives at the same identification by a different road. To seek, he says, simply means to pray, and he cites the Lord's own way of exhorting his disciples, where seeking and finding and knocking and opening are all plainly about prayer, the various expressions being drawn from common speech. He then widens the promise past the people addressed, since although the words are spoken to Israelites the doctrine belongs to the whole church, God having testified that he will be propitious to everyone who flees to him. The clause about the whole heart he explains as a necessary guard, because hypocrites are abundantly noisy and, when nothing but the external profession is looked at, appear to surpass the saints in zeal.

He also proposes a different conjunction. The particle before that clause is rendered when in the current version and in the ancient ones, with the Greek alone excepted, which has because; and Calvin observes that because is the usual sense and may stand here, since sincerity may justly be given as the reason why prayers are heard rather than as the condition attached to them.

On the gathering the notes are brief and turn outward. Clarke identifies the promise as a quotation from the older law rather than a new saying. Ellicott simply refers the substance and the fulfilment to what he has said on an earlier chapter. Gill defines being found as the moment when the favour is shown, the presence enjoyed and the thing sought obtained, whether the mercy be temporal or spiritual. Calvin sets a contrast between hiding and manifestation: God had in a manner hidden himself through the exile and then made his face shine out, and though he looks on us always, we do not see him and think him far off until we perceive that he is caring for our salvation. The promise to gather them, he adds, was framed to meet an obvious doubt, since they had no region allotted them where they might live together as one body but had been driven apart like chaff before a whirlwind, so that the question how they could ever be reassembled would naturally creep into many minds.
15:
The boast that provokes the passage is quoted back at the boasters. Ellicott takes the words for the claim of some exiles that they too had prophets, and preferred them; the answer sets the exiles in whom the prophet saw his nation's future hope against the worthless king and the people left behind, for whom sharper sufferings are foretold. Henry supplies the tone of the complaint, that the letter-writer was making himself busy and taking on him to advise men already satisfied with prophets of their own; and he names the impudence of it, that as the false prophets claimed their lies came from God, so the people who invited the flattery fathered that on God too, whereas anyone who hardens men in their sins with groundless hopes of mercy is plainly no prophet of God's raising up. Gill marks the turn more simply, the address moving from the godly among the captives to those who had believed the flatterers.

Clarke thinks the verse is in the wrong place. The Greek version, he says, very properly inserts it between the twentieth and the twenty-first, which leaves the connection here undisturbed and completes the connection below; and this is the second time in the chapter that he has reported a dislocation of the order without adopting it in his own text.

The threat against those still at home is read as a comparison meant for the exiles. Clarke puts it as advice not to envy the king on his throne or the people in the land they left, since sword and pestilence and famine are coming on them and a miserable captivity after, whereas the exiles have seen the worst of their case and hold a promise of enlargement at the proper time. Gill draws the same inference in reverse: so far from returning shortly, the men at Jerusalem would soon be captives beside them or dead. Calvin gives the purpose of the whole turn, that the captives might see the madness of promising themselves a return when final ruin stood so near both king and people.

Calvin then works the verb. To sit, he observes, is used in two senses here: the king sits in that he keeps his dignity, the people sit in that they rest and dwell quietly in a place. He explains why the throne is mentioned at all, since the exiles hung their hope on it, reasoning that while the temple stood and the kingdom continued it could not be all over with the nation; their safety seemed to rest on kingdom and priesthood together, and the promise that David's line should last as long as sun and moon made that splendour look like a guarantee. Only when it was extinguished could they be humbled. So the sentence tells them that though a king still sits on that throne, his case and his people's is harder than the captives' own.

The rest is handled in short strokes. Ellicott notes that the vile figs are borrowed from an earlier vision, but that the word here is not the one used there and carries the stronger force of horrible or loathsome. Calvin observes that the curses themselves come out of the older law, on his standing principle that the prophets drew the substance of their doctrine from that fountain and brought nothing strictly new, accommodating the doctrine of Moses to the circumstances of their own time; and he decides between two readings of the word for what the nations will do, preferring that they shake the head in contempt over that they tremble at the spectacle, so that all who see the ruin assent to the justice of it. Gill closes on the reason given: not hearkening to the prophets was not hearkening to God, and contempt of God and of his word was the cause of the whole ruin.
20:
Clarke opens with a division of the chapter he has taken from another hand. On that view there were two letters, the first ending here; the prophet, learning on the return of the embassy that the captives had received his advice coldly because false prophets promised them a quicker deliverance, wrote a second beginning at the fifteenth verse and continuing from the twenty-first, denouncing three of the chief offenders by name. It is the third time in the chapter that Clarke has reported a rearrangement of the order without adopting one.

Why the two men were killed is answered differently according to whose motive is in view. Clarke supplies a political reason for the king: predictions of a speedy deliverance made his Israelite subjects restless and might have provoked revolt, so he put the prophets to death, two of them burned alive, burning being a Chaldean punishment other nations borrowed. He adds the rabbinic identification of the pair with the two elders who tried to seduce Susanna. Gill agrees that the charges given here are not the king's reasons, reports a tradition that they had attempted the chastity of the king's daughter and were cast into a furnace for it, and thinks the real provocation was their prophesying the immediate fall of Babylon and stirring the captives to make ready for home; the crimes named in the text moved God to hand them over, not the king to burn them.

Calvin fixes on the manner of the death as the point of the prophecy. Had the death alone been foretold, the exiles might have doubted whether they had heard a prophecy; by naming the kind of punishment the prophet points as with a finger to something not merely unknown but incredible, since anyone might have supposed the king would kill them and nobody that he would roast them. He notes that the versions render the verb fried, and that the Hebrew word appears nowhere else as a verb, its participle being used of parched corn. On the curse he distinguishes the word here from the word used just before, the one an oath and this one a cursing.

Ellicott generalises the same clause into a habit of the language, the tendency to seize on individual cases of the highest blessedness or the deepest shame and work them up into set forms of blessing and cursing. Gill notes what the form implies about the men, that they had become so odious to people some of whom had taken them for true prophets. On the charge itself Ellicott observes that the Hebrew noun is almost always used of sins of impurity and more commonly rendered folly, and that the English villainy carried that sense for an older bishop. Gill lists the two offences, adultery and false prophesying, as the folly meant.

The closing assertion that God knows and is a witness draws out the best of the tile. Ellicott leaves open whether the prophet's information came supernaturally or by private letter from friends in Babylon, but suggests why the knowledge is pressed so hard: men with such narrow ideas of God had persuaded themselves he hardly exercised his power so far off as Babylon, so that they might sin there undetected, thinking of him as a God far away rather than near. Henry arranges the same guilt in ascending order: lying was bad, lying to God's people to delude them with a false hope was worse, and resting their own lies on the God of truth was worst of all; and he adds the motive, that they flattered others in their sins because they could not reprove them without condemning themselves. The most secret sins, he ends, are known already, and a day is coming that will bring to light all the hidden works of darkness.
24:
Ellicott marks the section off. These verses are a fragment attached to the letter for their associations rather than a part of it, standing to it much as a second apostolic epistle stands to a first. The letter had roused the rival prophets at Babylon, who organised a movement for the writer's destruction with Shemaiah at its head. Of the man nothing more is known, and the description attached to his name yields nothing, no place of that name occurring anywhere; Ellicott allows only a possible play on the Hebrew for dreamer. Henry adopts the play as character, calling him the dreamer because he claimed to receive his prophecies in dreams.

What Shemaiah did is treated as revealing. Henry observes that he neither defended his commission nor argued for his predictions, but wrote to the priests, the patrons of false prophets, and set them on to persecute, in his own name and without pretending the people's consent, by the very messengers who had brought the letter he was answering. Ellicott gives the aim: to make the deputy priest silence the prophet and punish him as a false one.

Who Zephaniah was and why he was appealed to occupies all of them. Clarke and Wesley both identify him as the second priest, and Clarke records his death at Riblah after the city fell. Ellicott adds the function that makes the appeal intelligible: as deputy it was his duty to keep order in the temple and punish pretenders to prophecy, and the letter reproaches his timidity in it, his conduct elsewhere marking a neutral position cautious enough for threats to work on. Henry reads the reference to his predecessor as flattery, the writer insinuating that he was raised to the office for such a time as this, and comments that hearts are wretchedly hardened which justify doing mischief by having power to do it. Calvin hears a charge of ingratitude, the impostor reproaching a man promoted beyond hope and before his time with making God an unworthy return, and draws the moral that Satan's ministers turn themselves into angels of light but cannot imitate God's servants closely, craft being very different from prudent counsel.

The word rendered mad is glossed by Clarke and Ellicott alike as the habitual term of scorn for the ecstatic rapture that came on prophets true or false. Henry presses the injustice: the characters of the false prophets are thrown on the true, so a man once given a bad name is run down as a matter of course, nobody proposing that he be examined for proof of his mission.

The complaint against the prophet turns on a phrase that may not mean what the English says. Ellicott points out that captivity has nothing answering to it in the Hebrew, and that some render the clause it is far off, either because the writer counted on the distance of Babylon to write with impunity, or as an abrupt summary: exile's end and homeland alike far off, so haste is folly. Henry keeps the received sense and turns the accusation round, since the false prophets had first said the captivity would never come and were proved wrong, which was reason to believe the man who said it would be long. Calvin defends the man accused: the crime laid on him was making the captives careless of their country, whereas his design was that they should not anticipate the promises but stretch their hope to the appointed end. Gill notes that the blame is laid wholly on the priests, who should have stopped his mouth and prevented the letter. On the reading of the letters Ellicott finds Zephaniah acting as his character suggests, not doing what Shemaiah wanted but using them at most as a warning; Henry thinks he protected the prophet and told him the contents so he might know what enemies he had among the captives.
30:
The sentence has two limbs and everyone counts them the same way. Keil and Delitzsch state them plainly: none of the man's children shall be left among the people, and he himself shall not see, that is not share in, the good the Lord will yet do; the extinction of his line and his exclusion from the day of redemption are together the penalty for rebellion against a commandment. Clarke divides the same thing into three, that he shall have no posterity to succeed him, that his relations shall not be found among those brought back, and that he shall not himself see the good; and he names the offence exactly, that the man had excited the people to reject the true prophet and receive the lying words of the false, who then led them into rebellion. Gill puts the ground more briefly still, that he prophesied without being sent and prophesied lies by which the people were deceived. Gill also notes when the word came, after the letter had been read aloud to the prophet, so that the answer follows immediately on the hearing.

Calvin makes something of how short the oracle is. The prophet does not argue; he simply declares by the power of the Spirit what is going to happen, speaking as a herald sent to proclaim a judgment, and the brevity is the point, because there was to be no dispute. It is the more striking, he adds, for the contrast: the impostor was carrying himself very high and did not hesitate to overthrow a truth that had been confirmed by many witnesses, and he is answered in a sentence.

The punishment is then fitted to the crime at both ends. Calvin observes that to be left without seed was a curse named in the law itself, so the first limb is a known penalty rather than a new invention. The second he reads as an exact reciprocity: the man had wanted to be home in two years where the prophet had commanded patience to the end of seventy, and for despising the appointed time he is shut out from ever seeing it arrive. He adds a remark about who the sentence was written for, since it did no good to Shemaiah or to his posterity, and its use was to work on the miserable exiles and bring them, however late, to repentance.

From the same verse Calvin draws the general doctrine he thinks the passage exists to teach. Nothing is more pestiferous in a church than that men should be carried away by a false confidence, because the foundation both of true religion and of our salvation is to depend on the word of God; and when a false trust draws us off, religion falls to the ground and every hope of salvation vanishes with it. The practical form he gives it is to embrace the doctrine that teaches trust in none but the one true God, and to reject the inventions that lead away from him even a little, so that a man neither looks about him nor is carried here and there.

Ellicott ends on the practical circumstances. The command to send implies a further letter to the exiles, carried in all likelihood as the first had been by envoys travelling between the two governments. No record of the prediction's fulfilment survives, but he takes its preservation here to imply that it was fulfilled, since a prophecy known to have failed would not have been kept. What strikes him most is the traffic itself: the frequency of communication between the two cities is worth noticing, both because it supports reading an earlier journey in the book as a literal one rather than a vision, and because it helps to account for the particular orders later given about the prophet's treatment when the city was finally taken.
